transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, hello, doctor. Thank you for fitting me in. I, um... I suppose I'm here because things have just gotten a bit out of hand lately. I teach secondary school, you see, so I'm used to a certain baseline of stress—grading papers, dealing with administration, the teenagers, all of that. You expect to be a bit wound up. 

But what finally made me actually pick up the phone and make this appointment is that my neck, my shoulders, and even my jaw are just tight almost all the time now. It's... it's like I'm constantly bracing for bad news. You know that physical feeling when you're waiting for something terrible to happen? It's exactly like that, but there's nothing actually happening. And it's not just when I'm in front of a noisy classroom, which you might expect. It happens when I'm just sitting quietly at my desk during a planning period, or, honestly, even when I'm at home at night. I'll be sitting on the sofa, trying to watch TV and just unwind from the day, and I'll suddenly realize my teeth are completely clenched together and my shoulders are practically hiked up to my ears. I have to consciously tell myself to drop my shoulders, but five minutes later, they're right back up there again. It's just this constant, relentless tightness, and I finally realized I can't just stretch it away or ignore it anymore.
Do you find yourself worrying excessively about a number of different things, even when there isn't an immediate reason to be concerned?

Yes, exactly. It's like... well, it's like my brain refuses to just sit still for five minutes. It's constantly flipping channels, and every single channel is a different crisis. 

Take the house, for example. We had some work done recently, and even though they finished up and everything looks perfectly fine, my mind just keeps jumping to whether the contractors missed something. I'll be sitting there thinking, what if they messed up the wiring? What if there's a pipe they nicked and it's slowly leaking behind the drywall and we won't know until the ceiling caves in? There is absolutely no immediate reason to think that, no water spots or anything, but I can't stop dwelling on it. 

And then, almost seamlessly, the worry just shifts right back to school. I start agonizing over whether my lesson plans are slipping this term, if I'm not giving the students the rigor they need or if I'm losing my touch. I sponsor the after-school robotics team, too, and I'll just suddenly be consumed with this absolute dread that the robotics kids are hopelessly behind the other schools in the district. They're good kids, they're probably fine, but in my head, it's a catastrophe waiting to happen and it's all my fault for not pushing them harder. 

And then... well, then it gets heavier, because I start worrying about my home life. I start thinking that I'm just completely disappointing my wife and my family by not keeping everything under control the way I should be. I'm 55 years old, I'm supposed to be the one who keeps the ship steered straight, you know? I should be a calming presence for them. But instead, my mind just keeps jumping from the contractors, to the lesson plans, to the robotics club, to whether I'm failing my family... just this endless, exhausting loop of worrying about things that haven't even happened.
When you're feeling particularly stressed or worried, do you notice any other physical symptoms, such as a racing heart, sweating, dizziness, or stomach issues?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I know what you're talking about—that sort of panic attack feeling where you think you're having a heart attack. My sister gets those, actually. She'll be in the grocery store and suddenly she's sweating and feels like she's going to pass out. But for me, it's not like that. It's not this sudden explosion of physical panic. 

It's more... well, like I was saying before, it's that constant, grinding tension. The jaw clenching, the shoulders. I don't get the racing heart or the dizzy spells. I don't find myself sweating through my shirts or anything like that. My stomach... I mean, maybe a little upset sometimes, but nothing I'd call an issue, really. Just the normal sort of indigestion you get when you're 55 and eat too fast between classes because you only have a twenty-minute lunch break and there's a line for the microwave in the staff lounge. 

So, no, none of those dramatic physical things. It's just... it's all up here, in my head, and in my muscles just refusing to let go. It's like my body is humming at this high frequency all the time, but it never actually boils over into a racing heart or feeling faint. It just stays right at that level of being completely wound up.
Do you feel like you're unable to control or stop the worrying, even when you know the thoughts are excessive or unrealistic?

Oh, absolutely. That is exactly the problem. I mean, I know it is excessive. I am a rational man, doctor. I teach these kids all day long, so I know how to be logical. I can stand there at the front of the classroom and literally tell myself to stop and just focus on the class in front of me. I will look at the thirty faces staring back at me and think, okay, just teach the lesson, be present. And I really, really try. But then... well, then just one tiny, almost insignificant thought will creep in. 

It could be anything, really. Like remembering a late invoice for some parts I ordered for the robotics team, or just noticing one student in the third row looking a bit lost and realizing they are falling behind. Just one small thought like that. And instead of just making a mental note to check on it later like a normal person would, it sets off this whole chain of what-ifs that I absolutely cannot shut down. 

I will be standing there mid-sentence, trying to explain the curriculum, but my brain is just racing ahead. If it is the invoice, I start thinking, what if the vendor cancels the order, what if the principal gets angry about the budget, what if the club gets shut down and the kids are crushed? Or if it is the student falling behind, I start worrying that they are going to fail the state exam, and then their parents are going to call a massive meeting with the administration, and I will be put on some sort of disciplinary review and lose my job, and then how will I support my wife? 

It just spirals and spirals. I try so hard to pull my attention back to the chalkboard, but it is like a runaway train. Once that first little worry pops up, it drags a hundred other catastrophes right behind it, and I am just entirely unable to hit the brakes. It is exhausting to fight your own brain like that all day.
Have you noticed yourself feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, like hobbies or spending time with family?

Well, no, not really down or hopeless. I mean, I wouldn't use those words. I'm not... I don't think I'm depressed, if that's what you're getting at. It's not that I don't want to do things or that I've lost interest. Actually, it's almost the opposite problem. I want to do all the things I usually enjoy, I really do. 

Like, take the weekends, for instance. I love working in my garden. I've got these raised beds out back that I built a few years ago—tomatoes, peppers, some zucchini that always gets out of hand. I usually love spending a Saturday morning out there just weeding and pruning. And I still want to do that! I'll go out there with my gloves and my trowel, fully intending to have a nice, relaxing morning. 

But the problem isn't that I've lost interest in the garden. The problem is that while I'm out there, my brain won't let me just enjoy the gardening. I'll be pulling weeds, and instead of just enjoying the sunshine and the quiet, I'm thinking about whether I submitted the right forms for the robotics competition, or if that leak I'm worried about is happening while I'm outside, or if I forgot to pay the water bill and they're going to shut off the sprinklers and ruin the whole crop. 

So I'm still doing the things I like, and I still want to be with my family. We try to have family dinners on Sunday nights, and I look forward to them. I don't want to hide in my room or anything like that. But I'll be sitting at the dinner table, carving the roast or whatever, and I'm just not completely there. I'm physically present, and I care about what they're saying, but there's this loud buzzing of worry in the back of my head that just distracts me from actually enjoying the moment. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I'm feeling hopeless or losing interest. I'm just... I'm just so preoccupied with all these worries that it makes it incredibly difficult to actually focus on and enjoy the things I still very much want to be doing. It's more frustrating than depressing, honestly. I just want to be able to turn the worry off so I can actually experience my life again without the constant background noise.
Do you find it hard to relax, even when you have time to yourself or when you're doing something you usually enjoy?

Yes, exactly. That's exactly it. Relaxing is... well, it feels like a completely foreign concept to me lately. Even when I have time, like a free period or a quiet evening at home, I just can't settle down. I feel completely wound up most of the day, honestly. It's this constant, vibrating energy, like I'm just sitting there waiting for the next shoe to drop, waiting for something else to go wrong. 

It's actually getting a bit ridiculous. I'll be at school, and instead of sitting at my desk grading papers during my planning period like I used to, I catch myself just pacing. Pacing back and forth across the front of the classroom, straightening desks that are already straight, wiping down the whiteboard for the third time. My colleagues probably think I've had too much coffee, but it's not caffeine. It's just this nervous energy that I don't know what to do with. 

And then between periods, when the kids are changing classes and it's absolute chaos in the hallways, I'm standing at my door, supposedly monitoring the hall, but I'm constantly checking my phone. I'm pulling it out of my pocket every two minutes to see if there are messages from the contractor about that leak at the house, or emails from parents, or updates from the administration. Even when I know there's no reason to expect a message right then, I just can't stop checking. 

So, sitting down and relaxing? Taking a breath? It just doesn't happen. Even when I'm doing something I usually enjoy, like I mentioned with the gardening, my body is just tense and restless. It's like my engine is idling way too high, all day long, and I just can't find the switch to turn it off.
